The raise and who is backing it

Town Lane Management has closed its second vehicle at $1.9 billion, more than a quarter above the original target. The fundraising, which kicked off in May, drew US commitments from endowments and charitable foundations alongside family offices and pension funds.

The new fund plans to write checks between $50 million and $300 million. Its predecessor raised $1.25 billion.

Commercial property funds have been grinding through a rough patch. Offices were knocked by the pandemic, higher rates have throttled dealmaking, and a JPMorgan Chase mid-year read shows values still about 25% below their prior peak. AI has boosted data center demand, but that lift has not fully offset broader weakness.

Town Lane is leaning into the gap. "Not having any legacy assets allows us to really be focused on playing offense today," said co-founder Tyler Henritze. "We have fresh capital for deals amidst increasing dislocation in the market."

Strategy, team, and deal flow to date

The first fund backed senior housing, retail, and industrial properties used by small businesses. As Henritze put it, "All of those sectors benefit from the fact that they're resilient in an AI world," noting "a real dearth of new supply" across them.

According to Henritze, Town Lane is also pursuing the AI wave by acquiring land in North Carolina alongside PowerHouse Data Centers in a partnership, aiming to construct a powered data-center shell that tenants can lease.

He and his sister, Parker Morse - an 11-year Sycamore Partners alum - started Town Lane.

Town Lane has added personnel drawn from TPG Inc., Starwood Capital Group, Coatue Management, and Blackstone. Tripp Johnson, a longtime TPG professional, holds the title of managing director, while Starwood alumni Andres Panza and Garret Overlock occupy senior investment posts. Former Blackstone leaders Michael Nash and William Stein sit on Town Lane's advisory group, joined by Guy Metcalfe, who for decades headed Morgan Stanley's real estate investment banking unit.

What it means for your portfolio

Bottom line: fresh capital without legacy assets meeting a market still marked by dislocation and lower prices. Watch where the firm deploys - senior housing, retail, and small-tenant industrial were its first bets, and data center infrastructure remains in focus. If values hover a quarter below prior highs, managers with dry powder and no baggage may find cleaner entry points.
